beforeRecord.q: A manager says positive output per worker proves that hiring more labor raises total output. At 10.5 workers, does the graph support the claim?

Average product is about 12 while marginal product is below zero; total output is falling despite positive average output.
Average product is about 15 while marginal product is below zero; positive average product proves that total output is rising.
Average product is about 12 while marginal product is below zero; positive average product proves that total output is rising.
beforeRecord.feedback: At 10.5 workers, the average product curve is near 15 while marginal product is negative. Average product measures the positive level total output/L; marginal product measures the effect of more labor. Positive average product therefore does not refute falling total output.
beforeRecord.imageAlt: Green average product (AP) and red marginal product (MP) curves, with an intersection near seven workers and marginal product crossing the zero line at ten workers. The plotted scale includes negative marginal product.

AP is shown only for positive labor. A guide marks the intersection at seven workers.

beforeRecord.q: Refer to the MP–AP graph. Between which two worker counts does MP cross AP, and why does the crossing locate the average-product maximum?
options: Between five and six; marginal output switches from pulling the average up to pulling it down.
Between four and five; marginal output switches from pulling the average up to pulling it down.
Between four and five; equality of marginal and average output makes total output zero.
Between five and six; equality of marginal and average output makes total output zero.
beforeRecord.feedback: MP is above AP at four workers and below AP at five, placing the plotted crossing between them. A marginal value above an average raises it; a marginal value below lowers it. Equality does not imply zero TP.
beforeRecord.imageAlt: Economics diagram: cop mp ap. Details are provided in the graph description.
beforeRecord.graphDescription: Workers are horizontal and product per worker vertical. MP at workers 1 through 8 is 8, 12, 14, 12, 10, 8, 6, 4. AP is the curve: it rises from 8 to about 11.5 by worker 4, then falls toward 9.25 at worker 8. MP is above AP at workers 2–4 and below it at workers 5–8.

afterRecord.q: Refer to the graph. At which whole-number worker count is average product highest, and why does adding the next worker lower it?
options: Five workers; the next worker adds less than the existing average.
Four workers; the next worker adds less than the existing average.
Four workers; the next worker reduces total output.
Five workers; the next worker reduces total output.
afterRecord.feedback: With four workers, total product is 46 units and average product is 46 ÷ 4 = 11.5. The fifth worker adds 10 units, below that average, so average product falls to 56 ÷ 5 = 11.2 while total output still rises. These are discrete worker observations; the intersection of connecting lines between workers does not identify the observed maximum.
